summary: Provides an analysis grid for evaluating and comparing GMPLS capabilities against the recovery mechanisms proposed in the IETF CCAMP working group. It analyzes each recovery phase using the terminology of RFC 4427. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A scorecard that compares different backup plans for a network, step by step.

subtitle: A scorecard for judging how GMPLS networks detect failures and recover traffic, from fast protection to flexible restoration.

tldr.problem: Several recovery mechanisms were proposed in the IETF CCAMP Working Group for GMPLS networks, and they needed a common way to be compared and checked against what GMPLS can already do.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through the five recovery phases defined in RFC 4427 (detection, localization, notification, recovery, reversion), classifies how recovery paths are pre-provisioned and how much spare capacity is overbooked, then scores the mechanisms on speed, robustness and resource use.
tldr.outcome: The conclusion is that these recovery types need only extensions to GMPLS signaling, and no GMPLS routing extensions. The document focuses on the transport plane, not on control plane resilience.

today: RFC 4428 is an Informational RFC from March 2006 and its metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its terminology comes from RFC 4427.

sections.title: Scope and the Five Recovery Phases
sections.content:
This memo provides an analysis grid for comparing the GMPLS protocol suite with the recovery mechanisms proposed in the IETF CCAMP Working Group. The concepts are technology independent, but the focus is on SONET/SDH, Optical Transport Networks (OTN) and pre-OTN technologies. It does not cover control plane resilience, and it does not specify protocols.

Using the terminology of RFC 4427, a failure of a label switched path (LSP) or span passes through five phases: failure detection, failure localization (and isolation), failure notification, recovery (protection or restoration) and reversion (normalization). The first three together are called fault management.

The term recovery covers both protection and restoration, and failure covers both signal failure and signal degradation. The RFC also separates horizontal hierarchy (partitioning) from vertical hierarchy (layering).
sections.eli5: When a road breaks, a good plan has five steps: notice it, find where, tell people, take a detour, and switch back when the road is fixed.

sections.title: Fault Management
sections.content:
Detection is the one phase the control plane cannot do alone, because it needs a hook into the transport plane. For example, SONET/SDH supervises continuity, connectivity, alignment, payload type and signal quality, and reports either Signal Degrade (SD) or Signal Fail (SF). Where an intermediate optical line system masks a failure, detection may be assisted by an out-of-band channel such as LMP.

Localization tells the deciding entity where the failure is and should start right after detection. Notification informs intermediate nodes and the deciding entities. Transport plane notices such as AIS can trigger protection switching directly, while control plane notices can trigger protection or restoration and need not follow the failed LSP's path. To avoid notification storms, alarms should be correlated and aggregated at the detecting node, sent only to a restricted set of destinations, and suppressed in case of correlated failures.

Correlation groups the many failures one event can cause, such as a fiber cut. It waits a failure correlation time, which the RFC says is hard to set by default and so should be configurable per node.
sections.eli5: First a sensor must notice the break. Then someone must work out where it is and tell the right people, but not shout at everybody at once.

sections.title: How Recovery Paths Are Provisioned
sections.content:
The RFC classifies how much of the recovery LSP is prepared in advance. The path can be pre-computed or computed on demand. A pre-computed path can be pre-signaled (reserving resources) or signaled on demand, and pre-signaled resources can be pre-selected or selected on demand.

It also classifies the overbooking of recovery resources as dedicated (1+1, 1:1), shared (1:N, M:N) or unprotected (0:1, 0:N, restorable only if capacity exists). Shared schemes can carry preemptible extra traffic. The RFC distinguishes recovery types such as 1:1 from schemes such as (1:1)^n, in which up to n pairs of disjoint working and recovery paths share one resource. That is called shared-mesh recovery.

For restoration, it defines times Tc (path computation), Ts (path selection), Tr (resource reservation) and Ta (activation). Restoration with a pre-computed route takes about Ts + Trs, and full re-routing takes Tc (+ Ts) + Trs. Pre-planned restoration reduces the post-failure time to just activation, Tas or Ta, while Tc + Ts + Tr or Trs is spent beforehand. The same ideas can be applied to LSP segments to cut recovery time.
sections.eli5: You can plan a detour long before the road breaks, or you can wait and figure it out afterwards. Planning ahead is faster but ties up a spare road in the meantime.

sections.title: Reversion and Hierarchies
sections.content:
Reversion moves traffic back to the repaired working path. Its use is the recovery domain's policy, and the ability to turn it off should exist. A Wait-To-Restore (WTR) timer prevents flapping from an intermittent defect: after the path is fault-free, a settable period, generally on the order of a few minutes (for instance, 5 minutes), must pass before traffic moves back. A path that cannot be recovered is an orphan and its resources must be released.

For hierarchies, a horizontal split divides a layer into recovery domains such as metro and core. A vertical split coordinates layers: the lower the layer, the faster the notification and switching, and the higher the layer, the finer the granularity. Escalation can run bottom-up, giving lower layers the first chance and using hold-off timers, or top-down. The RFC notes that SONET/SDH protection under 50 ms can sit on OTN restoration under 200 ms, so lower is not always faster.

A Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) is a set of links sharing a common risk, such as one fiber cable. Link and node diversity alone does not guarantee disjointness, and SRLG disjointness is necessary but not sufficient for survivability.
sections.eli5: After a road is repaired you wait a few minutes before sending everyone back, in case it breaks again. And two detours that share one bridge are not really two separate plans.

sections.title: The Analysis and Conclusions
sections.content:
Section 8 scores mechanisms on four qualities. Fast convergence concerns detection, correlation and hold-off. Efficiency is recovery switching time: the more pre-planning, the faster, so protection generally beats restoration, and SONET/SDH protection objectives are set at 50 ms in G.841. Robustness improves with less pre-assignment, but pre-planned resources cannot survive a failure that hits both working and recovery paths, so the two should be diverse in link, node and SRLG terms. Resource optimization depends on how recovery resources are shared.

The summary table crosses path setup (cases 1 to 3) with pre-planned or dynamic path search. Cases 1a, 2a and 3a prepare recovery before failure; 3b sets it up afterwards, which is full LSP re-routing. Pre-planned options are faster but less flexible, while dynamic ones are the most flexible and robust but slower.

The RFC concludes that implementing these mechanisms only needs GMPLS signaling extensions (RFC 3471 and RFC 3473), for pre-provisioning, failure notification, switching and reversion. No GMPLS routing extensions are expected to be needed.
sections.eli5: The scorecard compares plans on speed, toughness and how much spare road they use. Planning ahead is quick but rigid, and waiting is flexible but slow.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no additional security issue beyond those already present in GMPLS signaling, routing and management protocols. It does point out that authorizing requests for resources is a matter of local policy, which matters most for recovery schemes that share resources in advance or contend for resources in dynamic re-routing. Control elements should check requests against local authorization policy, based on the requester's identity verified cryptographically and/or topologically.
sections.eli5: When many users share spare roads, someone has to check who is allowed to use them. That is a local rule, not something this document sets.

items.title: 1. Failure Detection
items.text: The transport plane notices the failure.

items.title: 2. Failure Localization
items.text: Find where the failure is, and isolate it.

items.title: 3. Failure Notification
items.text: Tell intermediate nodes and the deciding entities.

items.title: 5. Reversion
items.text: Return traffic to the working path (normalization).

columns: What is set up before failure

cells: Signaled with resource reservation and selection
Called LSP protection; faster, less flexible, most resource-consuming
Pre-planned re-routing with pre-selection; only activation after failure
Pre-planned re-routing without pre-selection; activation and label selection after failure
LSP re-routing, full if path computed after failure; most flexible and robust, slower
